source: Lin et al. (2025) ZebraLogic: On the Scaling Limits of LLMs for Logical Reasoning (ICML 2025)
finding: Logic grid puzzles (CSPs with uniqueness constraints) were generated at controlled size. Accuracy collapses as the search space grows, even for strong reasoning models.
limits: Single puzzle family; 1,000 puzzles, sizes 2x2 to 6x6; complexity measured by search space size and Z3 conflicts.
agent_relevance: Un-aided chain of thought does not do constraint search at scale. Our scaffold should move propagation and search into code (O4), not into prose.

source: Lin et al. (2025) ZebraLogic, model-size scaling
finding: Bigger models help only on easy and medium puzzles. Beyond about 10^6 candidate assignments, extra parameters stop helping.
numbers: Llama-3.1-405B: 22.5% on Medium, 1.5% on Large, 0.0% on X-Large; overall 32.6%. Best non-reasoning model (Sonnet 3.5) 4.0% Large, 1.0% X-Large.
limits: Compares model families, not matched training.
agent_relevance: Do not expect a stronger base model alone to remove the need for explicit search structure on hard constraint problems.

source: Lin et al. (2025) ZebraLogic, repeated sampling and voting
finding: Sampling 128 answers from GPT-4o covers many correct answers (oracle selection) but real selectors gain little.
numbers: GPT-4o greedy 31.7 overall. Oracle best-of-128: 69.1 (above o1-mini 59.7). Majority vote N=32: 38.0 overall (Medium 81.1, Large 28.0, X-Large 2.5); more samples did not help further. Reward-model best-of-32: 34.8 (worse than voting). Oracle on Medium 92.9 at N=128.
limits: The oracle numbers need ground truth, so they are an upper bound only.
agent_relevance: Matches guardrail G4: agreement among samples is a weak signal. A code checker that verifies all constraints is what turns coverage into accuracy.

source: Lin et al. (2025) ZebraLogic, hidden reasoning tokens and self-verify
finding: o1 uses about 10 times more hidden reasoning tokens than GPT-4o, scaling with Z3 conflicts, but the scaling plateaus. Self-verification prompts gave small gains.
numbers: Mean hidden tokens: o1-mini 5,144.6, o1-preview 5,346.3 vs GPT-4o-mini 502.9, GPT-4o 543.7. About 400 hidden tokens per conflict below 20 conflicts; plateau above 30 conflicts. GPT-4o self-verify roughly 32-33 vs 31.7 baseline in the table rows read.
limits: Self-verify table rows were read from a garbled PDF layout; treat the self-verify figure as approximate.
agent_relevance: More thinking tokens help only until backtracking depth exceeds what the model can hold. Keep search state outside the context.

source: Chen et al. (2025) LR2Bench: Long-chain Reflective Reasoning via Constraint Satisfaction Problems
finding: 850 samples over six CSP tasks (Crossword, Acrostic, Logic Puzzle, Cryptogram, Sudoku, Drop Quote). Reasoning models beat chat models but still solve few instances exactly.
numbers: Average exact match: DeepSeek-R1 20.0, o1-preview 23.6, o1-mini 9.1, GPT-4o 3.2, Qwen2.5-72B 0.9, QwQ-32B-Preview 8.5. Average slot accuracy: R1 58.4, o1-preview 58.7, GPT-4o 43.7. Tokens: o1-preview 11,436 vs GPT-4o 1,486.
limits: Exact match is strict; partial match is far higher (R1 PM-0.5 62.0). Different tasks vary widely.
agent_relevance: Models get parts right (partial match) but fail on global consistency. A program that tracks and re-checks all constraints targets exactly this gap.

source: Chen et al. (2025) LR2Bench, failure analysis
finding: Repetition when a contradiction appears is the main failure. Models loop instead of backtracking and run out of length.
numbers: Strong negative correlation between 10-gram redundancy ratio and completion rate (CR). o1-preview beats GPT-4o on exact match by 37.5 points (Logic Puzzle) and 35.5 (Sudoku); QwQ beats Qwen-2.5-72B by 19.5 and 26.0. Cryptogram and Drop Quote: best model about 13% EM.
limits: Redundancy is correlational. Sudoku excluded from the redundancy measure.
agent_relevance: Impasse detection (a contradiction found) should trigger a code-controlled backtrack or restart, not more free text.

source: Amonkar et al. (2026) A Reality Check of Language Models as Formalizers on Constraint Satisfaction Problems
finding: Having the LLM write solver code (Python or SMT) instead of solving directly is not a free win on real CSPs. Formalizing lost to direct solving in most model-dataset pairs.
numbers: 4 benchmarks (Calendar, Trip, Meeting planning, ZebraLogic), 6 LLMs, 2 formal languages: formalizer underperforms solver in 15 of 24 model-dataset combinations.
limits: Workshop paper; evaluated on NaturalPlan and ZebraLogic style tasks only. Earlier versions (v2) had a different title and framing.
agent_relevance: Formalizing to a solver helps only if the translation is correct. We need a check on the translated constraints, not just on solver output.

source: Amonkar et al. (2026) Reality Check, complexity scaling
finding: Even though the search is done by the solver, formalization still degrades as the number of constraints grows.
numbers: With revision, Python formalization on the top 20% most-constrained problems scored under half of the 20% least-constrained in 10 of 12 model-dataset combinations.
limits: Calendar scheduling excluded as too easy.
agent_relevance: Constraint count, not search size, drives translation error. Extract constraints one at a time and check each.

source: Amonkar et al. (2026) Reality Check, error analysis
finding: Most formalization errors are wrongly defined constraints (information extraction slips), which the solver cannot flag. Reasoning models also reason like solvers inside the code step.
numbers: Wrong-constraint errors were 95% of Qwen3 semantic errors. Manual labels of 160 reasoning chains: under 75% (Qwen3) and under 50% (DeepSeek-R1) primarily code-related; solver-like reasoning used over 1.5x the tokens of code-related reasoning; up to 90% of R1 programs had unnecessary reasoning (hard-coded answers).
limits: Annotation of 10 examples per domain per formalism; small sample.
agent_relevance: Add a restatement check: re-read each constraint against the source text. Treat hard-coded answers in code as a fail.

source: He and Wang (2025) When Do Symbolic Solvers Enhance Reasoning in LLMs?
finding: Solver-integrated prompting helps on CSPs that need repeated backtracking, but chain of thought is better on shallow deduction and implicit-rule problems. Declarative exemplars matter a lot.
numbers: ZebraLogic (GPT-4o): CoT average about 28-33 (hard about 9-12); declarative one-shot Prolog average 58.8 (hard 44.0); declarative one-shot Python average 71.7 (hard 62.1). GSM8K: CoT 94.6 vs code 85.8-92.6 (CoT better). GSM-Hard: CoT 69.1 vs code 71-76.
limits: Table 2 was read from a garbled layout; row assignment of the ZebraLogic numbers is my best reading. Single dataset for CSP.
agent_relevance: Route by problem type: use a solver path for search-heavy constraint problems, plain reasoning for shallow or implicit-rule ones.

source: He and Wang (2025) Solver paper, size and retry effects
finding: A 13B code model with a declarative exemplar beats GPT-4o chain of thought on hard Zebra puzzles. Retries recover syntax errors but not wrong models.
numbers: Puzzle sizes 3x3 and 4x4: Claude 3.5 CoT 62.5 and 10; GPT-4o with code 90 and 72.5. GPT-4o Prolog one-shot ZebraLogic accuracy 83 at 1, 2 and 10 attempts (flat); CodeLlama13B Python one-shot 32 to 35 to 41. GSM-Hard Prolog zero-shot 49 to 71 with 10 attempts.
limits: 160 ZebraLogic cases in middle sizes for the retry table.
agent_relevance: Retries fix execution errors. They do not fix a wrong constraint model, so a semantic check is still needed.

source: Hazra et al. (2024) Can LLMs Reason? A Characterization via 3-SAT (later retitled Have LLMs Learned to Reason?)
finding: Random 3-SAT near the phase transition (clause/variable ratio about 4.267) is hardest for LLMs. GPT-4 shows solver-like easy-hard-easy behavior; other models do not.
numbers: GPT-4 SAT Search accuracy falls to about 10% in the hard region. Adding an external SAT solver via LLM translation (SAT-Translate) reaches about 100% across the whole range for GPT-4.
limits: Version read is v2 (Oct 2024). Search snippet says a later version found DeepSeek-R1 shows signs of learning; I did not open that version.
agent_relevance: Hardness peaks at the constraint-density threshold, so probe difficulty with density and escalate to a solver there.

source: Hazra et al. (2024) 3-SAT, models and format
finding: Changing input format (CNF vs menu) did not improve the models' own reasoning. The gain came from the external solver.
numbers: Format change: no significant improvement. Solver-assisted: near 100% for GPT-4; other LLMs improved similarly (appendix).
limits: Translation of 3-SAT is simple; real CSPs have messier language (see Amonkar 2026).
agent_relevance: Format polish is weak. Tooling is strong, when translation is easy to verify.

source: Michailidis, Tsouros, Guns (2026) DCP-Bench-Open / CP-Bench: LLMs for constraint modelling
finding: LLMs write constraint models more accurately in high-level Python frameworks than in MiniZinc. Documentation in the system prompt beats retrieved examples.
numbers: Zero-shot single-instance accuracy: Python frameworks up to 75%, MiniZinc max 57.3%. Level 3 baseline: CPMpy 70.1%, OR-Tools 68.9%, MiniZinc 37.8% (gpt-5.1). Retrieved examples (RAICL) lowered accuracy for DeepSeek-V3.2, Qwen3-Coder, Kimi-K2.
limits: The earlier v1 reported about 65% (Python) and 50% (MiniZinc), about 70% with best method; later version has a new benchmark and models.
agent_relevance: Prefer a high-level declarative library with its documentation in the prompt over bespoke examples.

source: Michailidis et al. (2026) DCP-Bench-Open, inference-time methods
finding: Repeated sampling plus self-verification with solver feedback gave the largest gains. Reasoning mode alone was inconsistent.
numbers: CPMpy single-instance accuracy gpt-5.1 70.1 to 90.2; Kimi-K2 66.5 to 89.0; OR-Tools up to +20; MiniZinc +35 for gpt-5.1 (37.8 to 73.2). Low reasoning: gpt-5.1 gained, gpt-oss and Kimi-K2 lost 5-10 points.
limits: Metric is single instance on the default example.
agent_relevance: Verification against solver output is the active ingredient. Reasoning effort alone is not.

source: Michailidis et al. (2026) DCP-Bench-Open, strict metric
finding: Models that pass the default instance often fail on other instances of the same problem, so models are fitted to the example rather than general.
numbers: On 23 multi-instance problems: SIA 78.3 vs MIA 60.9 (17.4 point drop); gpt-oss-120b and Qwen3-Coder SIA 69.6 to MIA 47.8 (over 30% relative drop); DeepSeek-V3.2 dropped only 8.7.
limits: Only 23 problems have multiple instances.
agent_relevance: Direct support for G3: a pass on the given example is not proof. Test on held-out instances.

source: Szeider (2026) CP-Agent: Agentic Constraint Programming
finding: A ReAct coding agent with a persistent Python kernel solves all 101 CP-Bench problems after the benchmark was cleaned, using a short prompt.
numbers: 100% on 101 problems in 3 runs with Claude Sonnet 4.5; 31 problem statements clarified; model success: Sonnet 100%, Opus 4.5 and GPT-5.1 97%, Haiku 87%, DeepSeek 83%, Grok 80%. A 50-line prompt matched or beat an earlier 800-line one.
limits: Benchmark was modified by the same author; ground-truth errors acknowledged by the original authors by personal communication. Not comparable to the unmodified score.
agent_relevance: Execution feedback in a loop plus a short strategy prompt is enough for a strong model. Avoid long procedural scripts.

source: Szeider (2026) CP-Agent, task management ablation
finding: Adding an explicit to-do tool cost tokens and sometimes hurt: it helped some hard problems and broke others.
numbers: Claude Haiku 4.5, 40 problems, 3 runs each: easy problems tokens +191% (15K to 44K), time +111% (18s to 38s), one more success; hard problems success fell from 52/60 to 45/60 (my reading of the text) with more overhead. Three hard problems fixed, three previously working problems broken.
limits: One small model; 40 problems; text near the table is ambiguous about the direction of the overall change.
agent_relevance: Extra bookkeeping layers are not free. Add them only where a measured gain exists.

source: Abdin et al. (2024) KITAB: Evaluating LLMs on Constraint Satisfaction for Information Retrieval (ICLR 2024)
finding: Queries like books by author X that satisfy constraint C show GPT-4 and GPT-3.5 fail to satisfy constraints, even when given the complete book list.
numbers: Over 600 authors and 13,000 queries. Irrelevant (possibly invented) items 12% to 41% without context. All-correct answers under 35% for both models. Complete context removed irrelevance but not constraint failures.
limits: Two models only (GPT-4, GPT-3.5, 2023); constraint types are lexical and temporal filters over lists.
agent_relevance: Giving the model all the facts does not make it filter correctly. Filtering by a constraint should be a code step over the list.

source: Abdin et al. (2024) KITAB, self-retrieval and scale
finding: Asking the model to first list all items itself raises irrelevant, fabricated items to satisfy the constraint. GPT-4 over GPT-3.5 was an improvement but not a large one.
numbers: Self-context increased the share of irrelevant books versus no-context; more constraints lowered completeness and satisfaction; the paper says the GPT-4 gain was not as dramatic.
limits: Exact per-condition percentages not recorded here.
agent_relevance: A model that is pressed to satisfy a constraint will fabricate items. Check each answer item against a source.

source: Seely et al. (2025) Sudoku-Bench: Evaluating creative reasoning with Sudoku variants
finding: Sudoku variants with unusual interacting constraints stump frontier models. Failure is in finding the first logical break-in, not in carrying on.
numbers: 100 puzzles (15 4x4, 15 6x6, 70 9x9). Single-shot solve rate all: o3-mini-high 14.0, Gemini 2.5 Pro 11.0, Qwen3-235B 8.0, DeepSeek-R1 6.0. 4x4: 40-73%; 6x6 0-13%; 9x9 0-2.9%. Multi-step (feedback after each digit) all: Gemini 11.0, R1 9.0, Grok 3 Mini 8.0.
limits: One evaluation per model per puzzle. May 2025 models. Multi-step mode helped small puzzles only.
agent_relevance: Propagation moves that no known rule gives (break-ins) are the hard part. This is where a reframing operator may earn its place.

source: Seely et al. (2025) Sudoku-Bench, failure modes
finding: Most common failure is a confident but wrong solution. Others: giving up, claiming missing information, claiming a contradiction that does not exist.
numbers: Failure categories named in Fig. 4: Incorrect Solution (most common), Surrender, Missing Information, Claimed Contradiction, No Reasoning Trace. Variants often have no starting digits, versus at least 17 in a standard 9x9 Sudoku.
limits: Counts per category are in a figure I did not extract.
agent_relevance: A claimed contradiction must be checked by code before the agent acts on it (G2).

source: Kaesberg et al. (2025) SPaRC: A Spatial Pathfinding Reasoning Challenge
finding: 1,000 path puzzles with rule constraints. Humans are near perfect, models are poor and do not spend more compute on harder puzzles.
numbers: Humans 98.0% overall, 94.5% on difficulty 5. o4-mini 15.8% overall, 1.1% on difficulty 5; GPT-4.1 best instruction model 1.6%. Over 50% of o4-mini outputs are invalid paths. Test-time tokens rose about 40% for non-reasoning and about 5% for reasoning models with difficulty. Multiple attempts: o4-mini 15.8 to 35.0. Prompt design 15.8 to 21.0; few-shot 12.6 to 15.8; image input 12.6 vs 5.6 text for o4-mini.
limits: Puzzle type is a single rule family (Witness-style). Human N small (100 puzzles annotated).
agent_relevance: Compute allocation should be set by the program from difficulty signals, since models do not scale effort themselves.

source: Bonlarron, Regin, De Maria, Regin (2025) Large Language Model Meets Constraint Propagation (GenCP + masked LMs)
finding: Text generation cast as a CSP with LLM-predicted domains. Previewing future-token domains with a masked LM improves solution yield on the COLLIE benchmark under strict constraints.
numbers: One-sentence task: vanilla 444 LLM calls, 375 backtracks, 3 solutions; metavar 456 calls, 211 backtracks, 4 solutions; previewMLM depth 2: 359 calls, 32 MLM calls, 170 backtracks, 10 solutions. Para-2: 3 solutions (metavar) to 6 (previewMLM); para-4: metavar 0 solutions, previewMLM 2.
limits: Small counts of solutions within a fixed time. Depth 3 and 4 gave fewer solutions in the same time. Benefit is for strong constraints; weaker constraints do fine without it.
agent_relevance: Real propagation (look ahead to prune domains) beats pure backtracking, but each look-ahead costs model calls. Budget it.

source: Dechter (2003) Constraint Processing; Mackworth (1977) Consistency in networks of relations
finding: Classical base: arc consistency prunes variable domains by local checks; maintaining it during search cuts backtracking. Cited by the LLM papers above (ZebraLogic and LR2Bench cite Dechter 2003); I did not open the originals.
numbers: Not recorded (from memory and citations only).
limits: Not opened this session. Verify numbers before use.
agent_relevance: Theory behind O4: propagate before you branch; choose the most constrained variable first.

source: Cheeseman, Kanefsky, Taylor (1991) Where the really hard problems are
finding: Hard instances of NP-complete problems cluster at a sharp phase transition in constraint density. Hazra et al. 2024 reuse this for 3-SAT (threshold about 4.267).
numbers: Threshold value 4.267 taken from the Hazra paper text, which I opened; the 1991 paper itself was not opened.
limits: Not opened. Threshold sharpness depends on problem model.
agent_relevance: Difficulty depends on constraint density; use it as an impasse signal.
